The paper develops a versatile VSVD semi-active suspension system combining variable stiffness MRE isolators and variable damping MR dampers for high-speed railway vehicles.
The scaled train model has a mass of 70 kg compared to the actual car body mass of 36,000 kg, with a weight ratio of 1:512.
The scaling factor used for the small-scale model is 1:8, derived from the formula 1:√512.
The secondary lateral suspension system includes four VS-MRE isolators and two VD-MR dampers.
MRE isolator stiffness increases from 4.18 kN/m at 0A to 8.32 kN/m at 3A, representing a 2-fold increase.
MR damper equivalent damping coefficient increases from 215.5 N·s/m at 0A to 704.8 N·s/m at 2A, more than 3 times increase.
The MRE isolator contains 10 layers of MRE round wafer bonded with 11 layers of mild steel.
The electromagnetic coil in the MRE isolator has 1000 turns with 1mm wire diameter.
The electromagnetic coil in the MR damper has 90 turns with 1mm wire diameter.
The force generated by the MRE isolator is calculated using: F = K'x + K''ẋ = G'A/h·x + G''A/h·ẋ.
The MRE isolator diameter is 35 mm with a thickness of 1.8 mm per layer.
The MR damper has an effective piston length of 30 mm and core radius of 7.5 mm.
The MR fluid used in the damper has a dynamic viscosity of 0.3825 Pa·s.
Four comparison suspension cases were tested: passive-off, passive-on, pure VS, and pure VD suspensions.
The control strategy for VSVD suspension is based on short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and sky-hook control.
MR fluid dampers require only small voltage compared to ER fluid dampers which require up to 8 kV/mm.
The paper evaluates suspension performance using both harmonic and random excitations.
The MRE isolator can replace the air spring in train suspension systems without major configuration changes.
The effective stiffness formula for MRE isolator is: k_eff = (F_max - F_min) / (D_max - D_min).
The energy dissipated by the MR damper in one cycle is represented by the area enclosed within the hysteresis loop.
The equivalent damping coefficient is calculated using: c_eff = E / (2π²fX₀²), where E is energy dissipated, f is frequency, and X₀ is excitation amplitude.
Testing results show that MR damper performance is not sensitive to excitation frequency variations between 1-5 Hz.
Testing results show that MR damper performance is not sensitive to excitation amplitude variations between 7-13 mm.
The paper demonstrates that VSVD suspension outperforms passive-off, passive-on, pure VS, and pure VD suspension systems.
The VSVD system can avoid lateral resonance of the car body by controlling stiffness while efficiently dissipating vibration energy through damping control.
